source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Setup: LLMs act as bandit agents with the task and full history in the prompt. Hard instance K=5 arms, gap 0.2 (best arm mean 0.6, others 0.4). Easy instance K=4, gap 0.5. Models GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2. Prompt varied in scenario, hint to explore, history format, CoT.
numbers: Bernoulli arms. GPT-4: about 50K queries; GPT-3.5 N=20 replicates over 48 prompt configs; Llama2 N=10, 32 configs. Main runs T=100, N=10-20.
limits: Power is low: N=10-20 and T=100 cannot separate good from bad by reward alone, so they use surrogate statistics (suffix failure, min arm fraction).
agent_relevance: Gives us a ready diagnostic for any in-agent explore step: did the best option get picked even once late in the run (suffix failure)?

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Headline: of all configurations tested, only one explored well: GPT-4 + hint to explore + externally summarised history (per-arm averages) + zero-shot chain of thought. Every other setup failed to converge to the best arm with significant probability.
numbers: One success config (BSSC0) among many; CoT with raw history failed.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small bandit, 2023 models (GPT-4-0613). Newer reasoning models were not tested here.
agent_relevance: Counts and averages should be computed by code and handed to the model (matches G5). Raw history in the prompt is not enough.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Main failure mode is the suffix failure: the model stops choosing the best arm and never returns to it. Basic GPT-4 prompt had suffix failures in over 60% of replicates (T=500); results are bimodal, some runs lock on the best arm, many never find it.
numbers: Basic GPT-4: >60% suffix failures. At T/2, all but five configs had SuffFailFreq >= 15%. Greedy baseline 0.47 at T=200, UCB 0.02, TS 0.00.
quote: fails to select the best arm even once after some initial rounds
limits: Bimodality hides the failure at short horizons: mean reward looks fine at T=100.
agent_relevance: Premature lock-in on the first good-looking branch is the default LLM behavior. A tree search needs a forced-revisit rule, not just a good prompt.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Second failure mode: uniform-like failure. Some GPT-4 configs avoid suffix failures but keep picking all arms near-equally and never narrow down. Measured by K*MinFrac (1.0 would be fully uniform).
numbers: Fig 4 GPT-4 table: K*MinFrac 0.03-0.49 across configs. The success config BSSC0 at T=200 N=40: K*MinFrac 0.29 (TS 0.23, UCB 0.12), SuffFailFreq 0.03, GreedyFrac 0.68 (TS 0.66), median rescaled reward 0.54 (UCB 0.70, TS 0.59).
limits: Success is judged against TS and UCB with 1000 replicates; LLM has only N=40.
agent_relevance: Two ways to fail: stuck too narrow, or never narrow. A per-class widen rule must also have a stop (narrow) rule.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Ablation: same winning prompt but raw history instead of summary (BSRC0) shows non-trivial suffix failures (0.12 vs 0.03). Summarisation, not CoT alone, carries the success. Also, GPT-3.5 is much worse than GPT-4 and Llama2 worse again; effects of single prompt edits interact and are hard to separate.
numbers: T=200, N=40, hard instance: BSRC0 SuffFailFreq(T/2) 0.12, K*MinFrac 0.11, median reward 0.65; BSSC0 0.03, 0.29, 0.54.
limits: Authors note summarising is easy for K=5 arms but not for many arms or contextual bandits where each context-arm is seen a few times.
agent_relevance: Supports having the program keep per-class counts and means. Warns that the summary trick may not scale to open-ended branches.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: BanditBench: multi-armed (MAB, K=10 and K=30, horizon 200 and 1000) and contextual bandits (MovieLens-based, 200 steps). 30 runs each, pairwise win-rate by t-test p<0.05. Compares raw history (RH), summarised history (SH), and algorithm-guided support (AG: per-arm exploit value and UCB explore bonus given in the prompt).
numbers: 16 MAB configs, 2 CB configs, 32 MAB models. Win-rate counts only significant wins.
limits: Models are Gemma-2B/9B and Gemini-1.5 Flash/Pro; no reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM can be handed the UCB bonus as a number per option and simply act on it.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: Inference-time UCB support helps big models and hard cases: MAB win-rate Flash 27.7 -> 32.2, Pro 45.5 -> 59.6; contextual bandit Flash 0.0 -> 46.4, Pro 7.1 -> 64.3. Optimal UCB reaches 90.6 (MAB) and 96.4 (CB). Small models (Gemma-2B 7.6 -> 4.9, 9B 10.5 -> 4.1) get worse.
numbers: Overall win-rate %, Table 1.
limits: Gain depends on model size. Table 3 (as extracted): Flash with AG at the small MAB setting fell 33.6 -> 26.6, while with more arms it rose 21.9 -> 37.9.
agent_relevance: Handing a UCB explore bonus to the model works only if the model is strong enough to use it. Gap to real UCB remains large (60 vs 90.6).

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: Algorithm distillation: fine-tuning on UCB trajectories (oracle behavior fine-tuning, OFT) lifted Gemini-1.5 Flash to 65.6 win-rate in MAB, above Pro's 45.5 with raw history. In contextual bandit, OFT on trajectories that include the UCB info raised Flash from 28.6 to 89.3, near LinUCB 96.4.
numbers: Win-rate %. Few-shot demos: Flash 27.5 (RH) -> 50.2 (SH); Pro few-shot RH 39.1, below its 45.5 baseline.
quote: few-shot examples we manually crafted could disrupt the CoT structure in larger models
limits: Few-shot hurt the larger model. Fine-tuning prefers raw history, few-shot prefers summaries. Training is outside our no-training rule.
agent_relevance: Our agent cannot fine-tune, so the usable part is inference-time AG. In-context demos can hurt strong models.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: Task difficulty of the demo matters in opposite ways: few-shot works better with easy demos (50.2 vs 43.0 hard), fine-tuning better with hard demos (65.6 vs 54.5 easy). Authors also fit a regret curve to rank exploration efficiency of models.
numbers: Gemini-1.5 Flash only, win-rate %.
limits: Single model family; small demo set (5 trajectories).
agent_relevance: Do not copy exploration demos blindly into the prompt; test on the agent's own tasks.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities
finding: Greediness: Gemma2 2B/9B/27B on 10-armed bandits cover only 40% / 65% / 65% of actions with CoT (about 25% without CoT); with 20 arms the largest model covers 45%. Up to 55% of the action space stays unexplored. Coverage stagnates after about 10 steps and regret stays above UCB.
numbers: Action coverage, 10 and 20 arms, Gemma2 2B/9B/27B, with and without CoT.
limits: Gemma2 family only; short interaction horizons.
agent_relevance: LLM branch choice collapses onto a few options. A widen rule needs a coverage floor per class.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities
finding: Frequency bias: 2B model copies its most frequent past action; with many repeats 96% of its picks are the frequent action. 27B model is much less affected (14%). Pre-training pull to repeat what is already in context.
numbers: Fraction of frequent actions vs repetitions in context, 10-armed MAB.
limits: Same pattern was seen in GPT-3 horizon task (Binz and Schulz).
agent_relevance: Repeated text in the context raises the chance the model picks it again. Show the model a deduplicated, counted view.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities
finding: Knowing-doing gap: 87% of the model's CoT rationales compute the right UCB values, yet 58% of actions are the greedy one (21% optimal) when the rationale is correct. The intro of the paper quotes 64% greedy. The model knows UCB but does not act on it.
numbers: 10-armed MAB, rationale checked against true UCB values.
limits: Two different greedy figures appear in the paper (58% in section 4, 64% in intro).
agent_relevance: Do not let the model both compute and choose. The program should take the argmax of UCB. Matches schema rule that code decides transitions.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities
finding: Fixes: RL fine-tuning on own CoT raises action coverage by +12% (2B, 30K updates) and cuts frequent-action share from 70% to 35%. Simplest prompt-level fix, forcing every action to be tried once (try-all, like UCB initialisation), gave the biggest gain and let Gemma2 27B almost close the gap to UCB. A +1 reward bonus for untried actions during RL raised coverage from 50% to 70%.
numbers: Comparison of 7 mechanisms: try-all, epsilon-greedy, context randomisation, context summary, self-correction, self-consistency, exploration bonus.
limits: Effects vary by model scale; epsilon-greedy and self-consistency were mixed.
agent_relevance: Try-all initialisation costs nothing and is code-controlled: visit every class once before judging it.

source: Park et al. (2024/2025) Do LLM Agents Have Regret? A Case Study in Online Learning and Games
finding: In adversarial, non-stochastic online learning, GPT-4 class models mostly reach sublinear regret and often beat FTRL/FTPL in repeated games, yet simple cases exist where GPT-4 is not no-regret. Authors add a regret-loss for training.
numbers: Tests over horizons T=100, 200, 500 against FTRL/FTPL; GPT-3.5 and weaker open models worse.
quote: Occasionally, GPT-4 even provides a negative regret value.
limits: Only the intro, method and results text were skimmed, not the proofs. The failing cases are ones with shifting loss trends.
agent_relevance: Regret is a usable audit metric for a choose-among-branches policy. LLMs track trends when the sequence is visible but can fail when it shifts.

source: Monea et al. (2025) LLMs Are In-Context Bandit Reinforcement Learners
finding: In-context RL on classification bandits (reward only, no labels). Naive ICRL gets stuck; two things make it work: enough stochasticity to explore, and keeping only episodes with positive reward. Stochastic ICRL randomly keeps each past episode with probability 0.1 instead of raising temperature.
numbers: Banking77, CLINC150, NLU, TREC, TREC-fine; models Llama 3.1, Qwen2.5 (0.5B-72B), Gemini 1.5 Flash. pkeep=0.1; pkeep=1.0 struggles.
quote: exploration is the key ingredient necessary for ICRL behavior in LLMs
limits: Which model each appendix table row refers to was not clear in the text extract.
agent_relevance: Randomly dropping context items is an exploration device that costs no extra calls. A candidate for shaking branches out of a rut.

source: Monea et al. (2025) LLMs Are In-Context Bandit Reinforcement Learners
finding: Numbers: CLINC150 final accuracy 0.104 naive, 0.648 positive-only (Naive+), 0.660 Stochastic (0-step 0.172; upper bound 0.944). NLU 0.292 / 0.836 / 0.814 (upper bound 0.844). TREC-fine 0.412 / 0.744 / 0.836 (upper bound 0.760). Regret on CLINC150: Naive 7126 mistakes, Naive+ 2280, Stochastic 4613.
numbers: Final accuracy and cumulative regret (total wrong answers); appendix table, one model per table.
limits: Stochastic is lower than Naive+ on some sets but can learn from negative rewards; models reason poorly about why an answer was wrong.
agent_relevance: Failures are weak teachers: the model learns from successes far better than from errors, which fits G2 (revise from real output, not from opinion).

source: Binz and Schulz (2022/2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: Horizon task (Wilson): two-armed bandit with 4 forced trials then 1 or 6 free trials. GPT-3 regret equals humans at short horizon (t(5566)=-0.04, p=.97). Over the whole experiment GPT-3 has lower regret than humans (M=2.72 vs 3.24, t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001).
numbers: Decisions from descriptions on 13,000 problems; horizon task compared with human subjects. Model: GPT-3.
limits: Regret advantage vanishes with practice: humans improve more within a task and reach slightly lower final regret (p=.23).
agent_relevance: A language model can do well on raw reward without any exploration. Good reward is not evidence of exploring.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022/2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: No directed exploration, only rudimentary random exploration. Effect of reward difference on choice noise was significant (beta=0.18, z=14.48), but no interaction with horizon (beta=-0.02, p=.14), so noise is not used strategically. Effect of horizon on picking the more informative option: beta=-0.15, SE 0.27, p=.58. Strong perseveration: prefers the option it saw more.
numbers: Unequal and equal information conditions, GPT-3.
quote: it shows no signatures of directed exploration
limits: Single 2022 model; later models not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Models ignore the remaining budget when deciding whether to explore. Budget awareness (horizon) must be fed by code, e.g. widen more when many steps remain.

source: Burda et al. (2019) Exploration by Random Network Distillation
finding: RND intrinsic reward (error predicting a fixed random network) avoids the noisy-TV problem of forward-dynamics curiosity because the target is deterministic. With intrinsic reward only, the agent finds more than half the rooms in Montezuma's Revenge; with two value heads the best agent often finds 22 of 24 rooms on level 1 and occasionally passes it. State of the art on Montezuma, Venture, Gravitar; on Pitfall! both RND and PPO find no positive reward.
numbers: Six hard-exploration Atari games; RNN policy.
limits: Dynamics-based curiosity oscillated between two rooms in Montezuma due to sticky-action stochasticity (noisy TV); similar in PrivateEye, Pitfall.
agent_relevance: Rewarding any novelty or prediction error attracts the agent to unlearnable noise. Prefer a novelty signal whose target is deterministic or checked by code.

source: Burda et al. (2018) Large-Scale Study of Curiosity-Driven Learning
finding: Pure curiosity, no extrinsic reward, across many game environments. Random fixed features work surprisingly well in training; inverse-dynamics features beat random features in 55% of Atari games and transfer better. A literal noisy TV added to a Unity maze drastically slows learning, though agents sometimes still reach the extrinsic reward if run long enough. Larger batch (2048 vs 128 envs) lets a curious agent in Mario see 11 levels.
numbers: Noisy TV test: IDF and RF features with and without a TV that changes channel on action.
quote: As expected the presence of the TV drastically slows down learning
limits: Random features are weak at transfer to new levels; curiosity can score below a random agent where extrinsic reward is uncorrelated with novelty.
agent_relevance: Noisy-TV is a real, measured slowdown, not only a thought experiment; plan a cap for returns on unlearnable sources.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019/2021) Go-Explore: a New Approach for Hard-Exploration Problems
finding: Names two failure causes of intrinsic motivation: detachment (the agent forgets promising frontiers because their novelty reward is used up) and derailment (random noise stops it returning to a good state before exploring). Go-Explore keeps an archive of states, returns to a chosen one, then explores. Montezuma without domain knowledge: over 43,000 points (about 4x previous best); with domain knowledge mean over 650,000. Pitfall: first algorithm above zero, mean near 60,000.
numbers: Atari Montezuma's Revenge and Pitfall.
limits: Needs a resettable or deterministic simulator in phase 1; robustification by imitation in phase 2.
agent_relevance: Direct template for tree search with state restore: keep an archive of frontier nodes, return to them deterministically, then widen. Prevents detachment and derailment.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: ELLM replaces count/prediction-error novelty with goals proposed by an LLM from the text description of the current scene. Of ELLM's suggested goals in Crafter, 64.9% were sensible, context-sensitive and achievable; about 5% were impossible by game physics; the rest broke context-sensitivity (13.6%) or common sense (16.4%) in the paper's breakdown. Novelty-only baselines (RND, APT, Novelty) averaged under 3 achievements.
numbers: Crafter, 5 seeds; goal quality table; ELLM vs RND, APT, oracle.
quote: not everything novel or unpredictable is useful
limits: Needs text captions of the state; hallucinated goals are filtered only by the environment's rules. The goal-quality table was garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: LLM can act as a 'what is worth exploring' prior, replacing raw novelty. Checking its suggestions against code remains needed.

source: Zhang et al. (2023/2024) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: Uses an LLM to say which learnable tasks are interesting, to avoid boring distraction. Crafter, tasks learned (success >= 0.2): uniform sampling 4, learning progress (LP) 55 (9 interesting), OMNI (LP + model of interestingness) 82 (14 interesting). Average success on interesting tasks: uniform 0.103, LP 0.52, OMNI 0.78. BabyAI: uniform 1 task, LP 4, OMNI 8.
numbers: Crafter and BabyAI with PPO agents; GPT-3 davinci used for interestingness. Confidence intervals in paper; OMNI vs LP differences significant at all checkpoints.
limits: LP alone is lured to boring tasks whose success rate fluctuates; OMNI depends on prompt examples. BabyAI absolute rates remain tiny (0.0075).
agent_relevance: Learning-progress signals can be gamed by trivial variations (a cousin of noisy TV). An LLM filter for 'is this new in a way that matters' cut that.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models
finding: LATS runs MCTS over LLM actions. Selection uses UCT: V(s) + w * sqrt(ln N(parent) / N(s)), with an exploration weight w. Values come from the LLM score plus self-consistency, with reflection on failures. HumanEval Pass@1 92.7 with GPT-4; WebShop average score gain of 22.1 with GPT-3.5; HotPotQA EM beats ToT and RAP.
numbers: HotPotQA EM (n=5 children, k=50 trajectories): ReAct best-of-250 0.42, CoT-SC 0.40, LATS n=1 0.48, ToT 0.49, RAP 0.54, LATS 0.63.
limits: Needs reversible states; a 5-fold tree costs more calls. Authors' own baselines.
agent_relevance: A working LLM-agent loop that uses UCB-style selection. Gives measured evidence that bandit selection beats DFS in agent search.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models
finding: Ablation shows UCT/MCTS selection matters. Replacing MCTS with DFS and LM-pruning dropped HotPotQA EM from 0.63 to 0.42 (drop of 0.21); removing the LM heuristic gave 0.37; removing reflection 0.58. At k=10 trajectories LATS and RAP both 0.44, ToT 0.34; LATS expands fewer nodes.
numbers: HotPotQA EM, ReAct base, n=5, k=50. Single benchmark.
quote: LATS requires every component and operation for optimal performance.
limits: Gains confound three things: UCT, LM value score, reflection; the exploration weight w was not swept in the tables I read.
agent_relevance: Support for keeping a value + visit-count rule over plain depth-first or greedy best-first. The exploration weight w is a free parameter to tune on our own tasks.
